title: Typeahead Ranked by Past Searches
statement:
Build the suggestion box of a search field. It knows a history of past searches and how many times each was searched. As the user types one character at a time, it suggests the past searches that begin with what has been typed so far.

  • AutocompleteSystem(sentences, times) loads the history: sentences[i] was searched times[i] times. Sentences are distinct and use only lowercase letters and spaces.
  • input(c) receives the next character. If c is a letter or a space, append it to the text typed so far and return up to 3 past sentences that start with that text, ordered by search count, highest first. Equal counts are ordered by plain character order, where a space sorts before every letter and a shorter sentence before any longer one it is a prefix of.
  • If c is '#', the user pressed Enter: the typed text counts as one more search of that sentence (it may be new), the typed text is cleared, and the call returns [].

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first one creates the system. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor). '#' is never sent when nothing has been typed.

examples.why: "cat" (1 search) misses the top three. After "car" is searched again it ties "cat toy" at 3 and wins the tie because 'r' comes before 't'.
All counts tie. "ab" is a prefix of the others so it comes first, and a space sorts before 'c'.
Nothing starts with "h" at first. After "hi" is entered, it becomes part of the history.

constraints: c is a lowercase letter, a space or '#'
hints: The simple version keeps a map from sentence to count and, on every keystroke, filters by prefix and sorts. Where is the repeated work?
A trie walks one character per keystroke, so you never re-match the prefix from scratch. Keep a pointer to the trie node for the text typed so far.

Let every trie node remember the sentences that pass through it with their counts. On each keystroke, step to the child and pick the top 3 from that node by (count desc, text asc). On '#', add 1 to the sentence's count along its path and reset the pointer to the root.

explain.intuition:
The suggestions for a typed prefix are exactly the sentences in one subtree of a trie built from the history. Typing a character is one step down that trie, so keep a pointer to the current node instead of searching from the root each time. If a step finds no child, the prefix matches nothing, and it will keep matching nothing until Enter, so the pointer goes to null.

To rank quickly, each node stores the counts of all sentences below it. Then a keystroke only has to sort that node's sentences, or better, keep its top three. Recording a search walks the sentence's path once and bumps its count at every node. This is how a search box in a web app stays fast as history grows: the work per keystroke depends on the matches, not on the whole history.
steps: Create a root node. For each sentence, insert it with its count: walk or create nodes character by character, and at every node on the path set hits[sentence] += count.
input(c) for a letter or space: append c to typed. If cur is not null, move it to its child for c (null if missing).
If cur is null, return []. Otherwise sort cur.hits by count descending, then text ascending, and return the first three texts.
input('#'): insert typed with count 1, reset typed and cur = root, return [].
pitfalls: Forgetting that after one mismatched character every later character also matches nothing. Without the null pointer, the next character may wrongly match from the root.
Getting the tie order wrong. A space (code 32) sorts before letters, and a sentence sorts before any longer one that starts with it.
Only incrementing the count at the last node when recording a search. Every node on the path stores the count, so all of them must be updated.

complexity.time: O(m log m) per keystroke for m matching sentences, O(L) to record a sentence of length L
complexity.space: O(total characters × depth) for the per-node counts

solutions.title: Count map, filter on every keystroke
solutions.idea: Keep sentence → count. On each character, filter all sentences by the typed prefix and sort.
solutions.time: O(S · L + S log S) per keystroke

solutions.title: Trie with counts at every node
solutions.idea: Each node stores the counts of all sentences below it. A pointer follows the typed text one character at a time.

followups: Keep a sorted top-3 list in each node instead of all counts. What has to happen when a count changes?
The history has millions of sentences and suggestions must come from a server. What would you cache in the browser, and how would you debounce requests?
